before.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
before.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. after.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
after.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
after.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Critical and feminist geography add questions about capital, mobility, gender and contested place histories; Hayden and the History Workshop journal show specific historical uses. after.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme. Harvey and Massey disagree within critical inquiry; neither stands for the whole discipline. Colonial frameworks are investigated as historically situated practices with internal conflicts. This expanded selection still does not represent global geography comprehensively.

before.label: Postcolonial history / critique
before.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak (1988); Dipesh Chakrabarty, Provincializing Europe (2000).

representative_people.context: Studies imperial authority through texts and institutions, combining discourse analysis with hegemony and attention to particular writers.
representative_people.works: Orientalism (1978)

representative_people.context: Questions intellectual representation through colonialism, labor and gender; uses deconstruction critically.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

representative_people.context: Tests European social-science categories against South Asian political histories while retaining their critical uses.
representative_people.works: Provincializing Europe (2000)

representative_people.context: Develops colonial historical difference through an explicit disagreement with Anderson.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines ambivalence, mimicry and hybrid cultural production; these concepts are debated interpretations.
representative_people.works: The Location of Culture (1994)

representative_people.context: Criticizes homogenizing accounts of women and develops historically situated feminist solidarity.
representative_people.works: “Under Western Eyes” (1984; revised 1991)

representative_people.context: Reworks Foucault through colonial archives, race and sexuality.
representative_people.works: Race and the Education of Desire (1995)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology examines the colonial production of authoritative knowledge in British India.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996)

before.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

before.label: History Workshop movement
before.description: Develops collaborative history from below through adult education, labour movements, and historical scholarship. Its socialist and feminist projects involve worker-historians alongside academic historians. Oral testimony, women’s history, and later work on popular memory reshape its concerns.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Raphael Samuel; History Workshop Journal (1976 onward); Sheila Rowbotham, Hidden from History (1973); Samuel, Theatres of Memory (1994); Gareth Stedman Jones, Languages of Class (1983), a contested reorientation in British social history.

outcomes.finding: Critical and feminist geography now have differentiated contexts. Hayden supplies explicit historical use of Harvey and citation of Massey’s criticism; Massey contributes to the1995History Workshop spatial-history section, introduced by Driver/Samuel. Harvey’s limited endorsement of local resistance is retained beside Massey’s critique of fixed tradition. Massey’s colonial/mobility argument and Driver’s contested imperial field practices prevent a uniform European/US disciplinary model. Gilroy and Said supply specific incoming resources.
outcomes.research_limit: Selected bounded cases, not global or field-wide coverage. Massey1991 complete article PDF text read;1995accessible OCR traversed throughout but has missing words and is not a full textual collation. Harvey302–304 visually read; full book and1991lecture unread. Hayden selected passages/notes only. Flexible Sexism author abstract and primary introduction excerpt read; Driver1992abstract only. Driver’s ten-page Hints article read completely, but manuals/archives not independently checked; issue1998 versus institutional1999 release dating left explicit. Workshop editorial coauthorship is metadata only; publication is not founding membership.
